strengths: Timely and important problem: safety mechanisms for text diffusion models (TDMs) are genuinely underexplored while diffusion-specific jailbreaks (DIJA, PAD) have recently shown severe vulnerabilities; the paper addresses a real gap rather than an AR-LLM-only concern.

Technically grounded method: the adaptation of the safe denoiser (Kim et al., 2025) to masked discrete diffusion is done carefully, including the derivation of the joint forward transition probability for absorbing-state diffusion (eq. 6), which is the discrete analogue of the Gaussian kernel and enables exact O(L) per-reference computation.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: three safety dimensions (hazard generation, jailbreak robustness, memorization), multiple TDMs (MDLM, LLaDA-8B-Base/Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-Instruct), multiple benchmarks, and composition with existing defences (PPL filtering, self-reminder, DiffuGuard) demonstrates modularity and breadth.

Useful ablations and efficiency analysis: sensitivity to η, the active time window, and negation set size, plus throughput measurements (e.g., 0.382→0.313 seq/s for LLaDA; sub-linear scaling in reference size) and a favourable cost comparison to FK Steering (matching k=8 safety at 34× lower wall-clock cost).

The largest effect (PAD ASR reductions of ~10–17pp across LLaDA models and benchmarks) is consistent across benchmarks and models, and the appendix honestly dissects cases where the LLaMA-Guard unsafe rate increases, attributing them to classifier style artifacts with supporting citations and corroborating ASR/refusal evidence.
Detailed appendices covering models, hyperparameters, metrics (with explicit formulas), negation set construction, and qualitative examples support reproducibility of the setup.
weaknesses: Overstated theoretical claim: the abstract and introduction claim generation is steered toward 'provably safe regions of the text space,' but the practical method uses Monte Carlo approximations over only N≈500–1000 references, a heuristic η replacing the intractable β*, and a truncated time window; the guarantee from Kim et al. holds only for the exact quantities, so the actual deployed method is heuristic guidance, not provably safe.

Modest and uneven safety gains: the headline hazardous-generation reduction is only ~5pp (38.4%→32.6%), and on DIJA—one of the two main diffusion-native attacks—reductions are frequently only 0.4–2pp and often within plausible run-to-run variance (e.g., 83.1→82.7 on AdvBench); DIJA ASR remains very high (~52–85%) under SAD, so the defence is largely ineffective for one of the main attack classes.

Selection-bias concerns in reporting: headline tables explicitly report 'the best-performing configuration (lowest ASR)' per defence, and η is tuned per model; without confidence intervals or consistency across configurations, the reported gains may overestimate the expected benefit.

Some circularity in the negation set choice: the best negation set (RTP) is drawn from the same distribution as the conditioning prompts, which the authors themselves note is a distribution-matching effect; this weakens claims about general safety improvements versus distribution-specific repulsion.

Modest methodological novelty: the core mechanism is inherited from Kim et al. (2025); the new derivation (eq. 6) is a straightforward categorical factorization, and the time-window/η heuristics follow prior observations (Kim et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). The contribution is primarily a competent adaptation plus evaluation.

Claimed 'diversity' preservation in the abstract is not substantiated: utility is measured only via BERTScore, PPL, and fuzzy overlap; no diversity metric (e.g., self-BLEU, distinct-n) is reported, so the abstract claim exceeds the evidence.

Memorization results are modest: fuzzy overlap decreases by only ~1–2.5pp (18.59%→~16–17.5%) even at η=128, and one condition (rand 0.03) shows zero improvement, while BERTScore slightly degrades at large η; the practical privacy benefit is limited. Additionally, evaluation relies on non-public code for (n,p)-extraction.
No explicit statement about releasing code or negation sets, which limits reproducibility for a method whose behaviour depends on reference-set construction and hyperparameter sweeps.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: safety of text diffusion models (TDMs) is genuinely underexplored relative to AR LLMs, and the paper motivates the gap well.

Breadth of evaluation is commendable: hazardous generation (RTP/ToxiGen/BeaverTails negation sets), diffusion-native jailbreaks (DIJA, PAD), memorization (fuzzy overlap plus (n,p)-discoverable extraction), and composition with existing defences (DiffuGuard, PPL filtering, self-reminder).

The discrete-diffusion adaptation is cleanly laid out: the categorical kernel factorization (eq. 6) replacing the Gaussian kernel of Kim et al. (2025) is a correct and sensible discrete analogue, and the prompt-agnostic negation-set design is a practical choice for modularity.

Useful ablations on the three hyperparameters (η, time window C, negation set size N), throughput analysis, and a comparison to FK Steering and Best-of-N showing a favourable wall-clock/safety trade-off (34× cheaper than FK Steering at comparable safety).
Honest appendix discussion of some inconvenient results, e.g., cases where SAD increases the Llama-Guard unsafe rate, with attempted explanations.
weaknesses: Overclaimed theory. The abstract and introduction repeatedly claim generation is steered toward 'provably safe regions of the text space' and that SAD 'provides formal safety guarantees.' The theorem (2.1) is inherited from Kim et al. (2025) and applies only to the exact unsafe denoiser and exact β*(xt). In practice both are approximated by a Monte Carlo estimate over N≈500–1000 references, and β* is replaced by a hand-tuned constant η times a crude estimate — none of the 'provable' guarantees survive this approximation. The paper never states what, if anything, is guaranteed for the deployed method.

Modest and inconsistent effect sizes. Headline hazardous-generation reductions are ~5–6pp (38.4→32.6% ASR on MDLM); DIJA gains are 0–7pp and sometimes negative (e.g., LLaDA-1.5 HarmBench DIJA 50.7→53.5); η-sensitivity figures (Figs. 2, 4) are visibly non-monotone and erratic, contradicting the text's claim of a 'consistent monotonic trend.' Many cells show near-zero or adverse changes.

Alarming refusal-rate collapse that is not convincingly resolved. Across all instruction-tuned models, refusal rates drop catastrophically with SAD (e.g., 87.4→6.6% on LLaDA-Instruct zero-shot, 99.6→3.5% on AdvBench, with corresponding increases in Llama-Guard unsafe rate up to +7.8pp). The appendix attributes this to classifier artifacts from 'style shift', citing one workshop paper. A defence that silently disables refusal behaviour while safety-classifier unsafe rates rise is a serious potential harm; the paper's own Impact Statement does not address this adequately, and no human evaluation is provided to substantiate the 'false positive' explanation.

Evaluation methodology concerns. (i) Table captions state that 'entries are the best-performing configuration (lowest ASR) under each defence' — per-cell selection of the best hyperparameter configuration inflates results and invites overfitting to the test set. (ii) HarmBench is used simultaneously as the negation set source (LLaMA-generated harmful completions) and the ASR judge, creating a train-on-test-style leakage concern for the jailbreak results, particularly the large PAD gains. (iii) Utility evaluation is weak: BERTScore on benign prompts is acknowledged to be expected to change ~0, so it cannot demonstrate preserved quality under intervention; no diversity metric is reported despite the abstract claiming preserved 'diversity.'

Limited novelty. The method is a direct port of Kim et al. (2025)'s safe denoiser to masked discrete diffusion; the paper itself frames it as 'adopt and modify.' The genuinely new technical content (eq. 6, prompt clamping, time-window schedule) is thin, and concurrent works (DiffuGuard, ILRR) cover adjacent ground with clearer differentiation needed.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness: baseline ASR reported as 38.4% (Table 1) vs 37.8% (Table 6) and 20.8% vs 19.8% for LLaDA under nominally the same setting; typo-laden text ('obsered', 'is lower is better', equation numbering referencing 'eq 4 and eq 5' with a misplaced footnote); Table 4 claims LLaDA hazard experiment 'T = 256' where a generation length L was clearly meant. These undermine confidence in experimental bookkeeping.

Reproducibility is partial at best: no code release is mentioned, and a key evaluation relies on non-public code shared by third-party authors (Luo et al. (2026) extraction framework). Many headline tables lack error bars or significance tests, and one comparison uses only 100 prompts (Appendix C.2).

The memorization result is confined to a WikiText-103 fine-tuned MDLM with the negation set drawn from the same training distribution; generalization to realistic pretraining-scale memorization (e.g., PII) is not demonstrated, and fuzzy-overlap reductions (~1–2.5pp) are small relative to the claimed significance.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: safety mechanisms for text diffusion models (TDMs), where existing AR-oriented safeguards do not transfer and diffusion-native jailbreaks (DIJA, PAD) show high attack success rates.

Provides a clean adaptation of the continuous-state safe denoiser (Kim et al., 2025) to masked discrete diffusion, including a correct derivation of the joint forward kernel (eq. 6) that replaces the Gaussian kernel with an O(L) match-count computation, and a sensible prompt-agnostic conditioning design that keeps a single negation set universal across prompts.

Comprehensive empirical coverage across three threat models (hazardous generation, jailbreaks, memorization), multiple TDMs (MDLM, LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-Instruct), multiple negation sets, and multiple composed defences (PPL filtering, self-reminder, DiffuGuard).

Useful ablations and efficiency analysis: saturation of safety gains at N≈500–1000 references, sensitivity to guidance scale η and active time-window C, and throughput measurements showing sub-linear cost in reference size (at most 2.3% overhead from 100→5000 references).

Favourable cost comparison against FK Steering (matching safety at ~34× lower wall-clock cost) and a convincing discussion of why Best-of-N cannot repair early trajectory commitment under PAD attacks.

Honest limitations discussion in places, including an explicit appendix analysis (C.4) of conditions where SAD increases LLaMA-Guard unsafe rate, attributing it to style-shift classifier artifacts corroborated by HarmBench ASR.
weaknesses: Overstated theoretical claims. The abstract and introduction repeatedly claim samples are steered toward 'provably safe' regions and that 'SAD provides formal safety guarantees' (vs. DiffuGuard's heuristics). However, the deployed method (i) replaces the exact weight β*(x_t) with a hyperparameter-scaled approximation η·β(x_t), (ii) uses a finite Monte Carlo negation set of N≈500–1000 samples that cannot represent the true unsafe set over a vocabulary-sized text space, and (iii) imports Theorem 2.1 verbatim from the continuous setting of Kim et al. (2025). The guarantees hold only for the idealized quantity, not the deployed intervention; the safety framing should be softened substantially.

Modest and uneven effect sizes. Hazardous-generation ASR drops only ~5–6 pp (e.g., 38.4%→32.6% on MDLM). Jailbreak gains are concentrated on PAD (−10 to −17 pp) but are small or absent on DIJA (often ≤2 pp, sometimes increases, e.g., +2.8 on LLaDA-1.5 HarmBench). Memorization improvements in fuzzy overlap are only ~1–2.5 pp, and Table 9 shows zero improvement in the rand 0.03 extraction condition.

Selection bias in headline results. Table notes state 'Entries are the best-performing configuration (lowest ASR) under each defence,' and headline jailbreak numbers are reported on the best configuration per defence/model. This inflates reported gains; a pre-registered fixed configuration with confidence intervals across seeds would be more trustworthy.

A dramatic and under-examined behavioural side effect: refusal rates collapse by 60–96 points under SAD (e.g., LLaDA-Instruct zero-shot refusal 87.4%→6.6%; AdvBench 99.6%→3.5%). The paper frames the associated LLaMA-Guard unsafe-rate increases as classifier artifacts, but such a large shift from refusal to 'topical engagement' is a substantive change in model behavior that may generalize poorly beyond the tested attacks and deserves more careful treatment than an appendix note.

The memorization mechanism is under-explained: repelling generation from only 500–1000 randomly sampled training sequences is claimed to reduce memorization of training data broadly, but why guidance from a tiny random subset generalizes to the full training distribution is not analyzed.

Limited baseline coverage: the training-free comparison (FK Steering, Best-of-N) is run only on MDLM with 100 RTP prompts, so the 'outperforming existing methods' claim rests on a narrow comparison; no comparison with Schiff et al. (2025) guidance or ILRR is empirical.

Presentation issues: several equations are garbled or referenced by bare numbers (eq 4/eq 5, the β(x_t) definition in Sec. 3.2), 'RPT' typo, and the notation table is confined to the appendix. The core novelty—porting an existing continuous method to the discrete setting—is solid but incremental, so the writing precision matters for the contribution's credibility.

strengths: Addresses a timely and genuinely underexplored problem: inference-time safety control for masked text diffusion models, where existing AR-oriented safety techniques do not directly transfer.

Provides a careful adaptation of the safe-denoiser identity (Kim et al., 2025) to discrete masked diffusion, including a clean derivation of the sequence-level categorical forward kernel (eq. 7) and an exact O(L) per-reference compatibility computation.

Unusually transparent treatment of the theory–practice gap: Appendix A explicitly documents every departure from the exact identity (relaxed kernel, length normalization, logit-space update, clamping), and Appendix F candidly discusses that the one-sided ηβ̂ loses the posterior-odds interpretation and that no approximation bound is established.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three safety dimensions (hazard taxonomy, jailbreak robustness, memorization) on four models (MDLM, LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-Instruct), five jailbreak benchmarks, composition with existing defences (PPL, self-reminder, DiffuGuard), throughput analysis, and hyperparameter ablations.

Notable honesty about negative results: Appendix D dissects cases where SAD *increases* classifier-flagged unsafe rates, explains plausible mechanisms (style-shift false positives, small-benchmark variance), and even includes a deliberately retained negative qualitative example (Example 2) that its own judge scores as safe.
Favourable efficiency profile: matches FK Steering (k=8) unsafe rate at ~29× lower wall-clock cost with better perplexity, and safety gains plateau at a practical negation-set size of N≈500–1000.
weaknesses: Effect sizes are modest and inconsistent. The headline hazardous-generation reduction is ~5 points (38.4%→32.6% on MDLM; 19.8%→14.8% on LLaDA), DIJA gains are often 1–7 points and occasionally negative, and several zero-shot conditions show increased unsafe rates (e.g., +7.8pp for LLaDA-Instruct on HarmBench). The abstract's claim of steering toward 'provably safe regions' is not supported by the practical instantiation, which the paper itself concedes is not a safety certificate.

The strongest safety gains appear to depend on distribution matching: RTP as the negation set works best precisely when the conditioning prompts come from RTP (Appendix C.2). This raises the concern that the method repels the specific conditioning distribution rather than providing general safety, which weakens the generality of the central claim.

A large unexplained confound: refusal rates collapse under SAD (e.g., 87.4%→6.6% on LLaDA-Instruct WildJailbreak, 99.6%→3.5% on AdvBench). The paper acknowledges automatic judges are style-sensitive in both directions but performs no human annotation to separate genuine safety improvement from judge artifacts or 'compliant-but-harmless' behaviour, despite listing it as future work.

On several benchmarks the headroom argument undercuts the contribution: PPL filtering already suppresses ASR to near zero in some conditions, and DiffuGuard provides comparable or larger standalone gains; SAD's incremental value is clearest mainly for PAD-style early-commitment attacks.

Originality is moderate: the core mechanism is a direct transfer of Kim et al. (2025) to discrete diffusion, and the key new derivation (eq. 7) is a straightforward factorization. Two concurrent works (Lee & Han 2026; An & Han 2026) pursue very similar inference-time safety steering for masked diffusion LMs, and no empirical comparison against them is provided.

Hyperparameters do not transfer across models and negation sets (η is retuned per model, non-monotone behaviour at large η), and headline tables report the best-performing configuration per defence, which inflates apparent robustness relative to a single pre-registered setting.

strengths: Targets a timely and genuinely underexplored problem: safety mechanisms for text diffusion models, where diffusion-native jailbreaks (DIJA, PAD) are very recent and existing AR-oriented defences do not transfer directly.

The evaluation breadth is above average for this area: three TDM families (MDLM, LLaDA/LLaDA-1.5, Dream-Instruct), three safety dimensions (hazard taxonomy, jailbreak robustness, memorization), five jailbreak benchmarks, and composition with existing defences (PPL filtering, self-reminder, DiffuGuard).
The efficiency comparison is a real selling point: SAD matches FK Steering (k=8) on unsafe rate at ~29x lower wall-clock cost (Table 8), which is practically meaningful.

The limitations discussion is unusually honest: Appendix F explicitly acknowledges the one-sided guidance coefficient, the absence of an approximation bound, negation-set coverage issues, and reliance on classifier-based judges; Appendix D includes a deliberately retained negative example (Example 2) showing a partially-mitigated output scored as safe.
Appendix A carefully documents the three departures of the practical estimator from the exact identity (relaxed kernel, length-normalized log scores, logit-space update), which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The refusal rate collapse is the most serious problem: across models and benchmarks, SAD reduces zero-shot refusal rates by tens of points (e.g., 87.4% to 6.6% on LLaDA-Instruct WildJailbreak; 99.6% to 3.5% on AdvBench, Table 12/13). For a safety paper, eliminating refusal behaviour is a major side effect. The authors attribute this to a 'style shift' using prior work on judge false positives, but concede they cannot rule out genuine degradation without human annotation — and no human evaluation is provided. A reader cannot tell whether SAD makes models safer or merely makes them stop refusing.

Effect sizes are modest, inconsistent, and concentrated on one attack: the headline hazardous-generation gain is ~5pp on MDLM and less on LLaDA (Table 1); on DIJA the changes are often near zero or negative (e.g., LLaDA-1.5 AdvBench DIJA +0.6, HarmBench DIJA +2.8 in ASR terms, Table 10). The main consistent gains come from PAD, and even there large negation-set-dependent variance remains.

The theoretical grounding is largely inherited: Theorem 2.1 is quoted directly from Kim et al. (2025), and the practical method (relaxed kernel, one-sided eta*beta-hat, logit-space update, hard timestep window) departs from it with no approximation bound, with acknowledged non-monotone behaviour in eta. The genuinely new derivation (the categorical kernel of eq. 7) is a straightforward substitution into a factorized forward process.

Results are reported as 'best-performing configuration (lowest ASR/unsafe rate) under each defence' (table notes), i.e., per-cell hyperparameter selection over a large sweep of eta, C, and N. Combined with fixed seeds, 'error bars when available', and the acknowledged ±1-3pp sampling variance on ~100-prompt benchmarks (Appendix D), this inflates headline numbers and undermines confidence in the small margins that carry the paper's claims.

All safety conclusions rest on automatic judges (Llama-Guard-3-8B, HarmBench classifier, regex refusal detection) that the paper itself shows are sensitive to style shifts 'in both directions'. Multiple judges mitigate but do not resolve this; the core claim that SAD 'substantially reduces unsafe generations' is therefore weakly supported where the gains are small.

The negation-set choice dominates the results and borders on distribution matching: the best hazardous-generation result uses RTP as the negation set against RTP-derived malicious prompts (Appendix C.2), which is close to fitting the test condition distribution rather than demonstrating general safety.

Presentation issues reduce polish: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('Code is available at' with no URL), the pseudo-perplexity equation (eq. 19 in Appendix B.7) repeats the AR expression and the surrounding text refers to 'not comparable to 19' when it means 18, and the paper cites several 2026 concurrent/preprint works as load-bearing baselines.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: safety interventions specifically designed for masked text diffusion models (MDLM, LLaDA, Dream) rather than transplanted AR-model heuristics, and the discrete-kernel derivation (eq. 7) for the unsafe denoiser is a clean, correct adaptation of the continuous safe-denoiser identity.

Unusually comprehensive empirical coverage for this space: three safety dimensions (hazard taxonomy, jailbreak robustness against diffusion-native attacks DIJA/PAD, and memorization via both fuzzy overlap and the (n,p)-discoverable extraction framework), five models, five jailbreak benchmarks, and composition with DiffuGuard, PPL filtering, and self-reminder.
The comparison to FK Steering is informative (matching unsafe rate at ~29x lower wall-clock), and the throughput analysis of overhead (Fig. 3, App. C.1) is a useful practical contribution.

The limitations discussion (Sec. 6 and especially Appendix F) is exceptionally honest and substantive, e.g., explicitly acknowledging that the practical estimator departs from the exact identity, that beta-hat drops the safe-side odds term, and that no finite-N or kernel-mismatch bound is established. Appendix D's analysis of judge artifacts, including retaining a deliberately negative qualitative example, reflects scientific integrity.
Code, hyperparameters, seeds, and protocol details (timestep convention conversion, negation set construction) are documented at a level that supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core method is a direct port of Kim et al. (2025)'s safe denoiser from image to text diffusion. The theoretical content (Thm 2.1) is entirely prior work; the paper's contribution is the discrete kernel, the practical estimator, and the empirical study. Concurrent works (Lee & Han 2026; An & Han 2026) pursue very similar ideas, and no head-to-head comparison with them is provided.

The gap between theory and practice is large: the deployed method replaces the exact kernel with a relaxed surrogate (eq. 8), length-normalized biased scores (eq. 10), a one-sided eta-tuned coefficient, and a logit-space update (eq. 11). The abstract's claim that samples are 'steered toward provably safe regions' overstates what the implemented method guarantees; the paper concedes it is 'not a safety certificate,' but the framing overpromises.

Safety gains are modest and inconsistent: 5-6pp ASR reductions in Table 1, ASR remaining above 50% for DIJA in many configurations, occasional negative effects (Dream PAD, several DIJA conditions), and non-monotone, noisy eta-sensitivity curves (Figs. 3-4) with no confidence intervals on headline tables. Some reported differences may be within run-to-run variance, especially on ~100-prompt benchmarks.

A serious unaddressed side effect: refusal rates collapse across the board (e.g., LLaDA-Instruct zero-shot 87.4% to 6.6%; LLaDA-1.5 83.0% to 6.0%; AdvBench 99.6% to ~4%). This is a dramatic behavioural change to instruction-tuned models that is only partly attributed to classifier style artifacts; the paper cannot rule out genuine degradation (it says so), and the practical consequence of near-total loss of refusal behaviour deserves more prominent treatment than an appendix note.

Potential evaluation circularity: the jailbreak negation set is constructed from HarmBench responses, and headline robustness is partly evaluated on HarmBench prompts, creating an in-distribution advantage that could inflate PAD gains; a fully held-out negation/evaluation split is not controlled for.

All safety and quality judgments are automated (Llama-Guard, HarmBench classifier, BERTScore, GPT-2 perplexity); no human evaluation of either harmfulness or utility is performed, and BERTScore on benign prompts is a weak utility proxy.

Headline baseline comparisons with training-free methods are limited to MDLM with 100 RTP prompts (Table 8); the memorization experiments use only a small WikiText-103 fine-tuned MDLM, limiting external validity for large-scale TDMs.
